title: The Power Sum
directAnswer: Count the ways to write X as a sum of **unique** natural numbers each raised to the power N (e.g. 100 = 10² = 6²+8² = 1²+3²+4²+5²+7² → 3 ways). Recurse over candidate bases in increasing order with an include/exclude choice: at base `b`, either use `b^N` (subtract it and move to `b+1`) or skip `b` (move to `b+1`). Base cases: if `b^N == remaining` count 1, if `b^N > remaining` count 0. Uniqueness is free because each base is considered exactly once and the base only increases. Time is O(2^m) where m = ⌊X^(1/N)⌋ bases.

remember.pattern: Increasing-base include/exclude recursion (each base used at most once)
rules: Always **advance the base** (`base + 1`) in both branches — that's what guarantees each natural is used at most once (uniqueness for free).
Two base cases: `base^N == remaining` returns **1** (found a combination); `base^N > remaining` returns **0** (prune, since later bases are even larger).
Start the recursion at **base = 1**, remaining = X.
The **include** branch subtracts `base^N`; the **exclude** branch leaves `remaining` unchanged. Both then move to `base + 1`.
You return a **count**, not the combinations themselves — no path array needed, just sum the two branches.
whenToUse: Count subsets of a fixed candidate set that hit an exact target
Each element usable at most once, order irrelevant (combinations, not permutations)
Candidates are generated on the fly (here, perfect powers) and naturally bounded
antiSignals: Elements may be reused unlimited times → don't advance the base in the include branch (that's coin-change style)
You need the actual combinations, not just the count → carry a path and record at the exact-hit leaf
Order matters / arrangements wanted → that's permutations, not this subset count
X or the candidate count is large with overlapping subproblems → memoize on (remaining, base)
remember.takeaway: The Power Sum is the canonical include/exclude subset-sum recursion with one twist: candidates are perfect powers and the base only moves forward, so uniqueness comes for free. Master 'subtract-and-advance OR skip-and-advance' here and Subsets, Combination Sum, and Partition all reuse it.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model 'sum of unique powers equal to X' as an include/exclude recursion over an increasing base, with correct exact-hit and overflow base cases, and recognise that advancing the base enforces uniqueness.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Allowing a base to be reused (not advancing in the include branch), restarting the base from 1 each call (producing permutations / duplicates), or wrong base cases (e.g. continuing after `base^N > remaining`).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that the base monotonically increases so each natural appears at most once, prune the moment `base^N > remaining`, and note this is subset-sum's count variant — mention memoization on (remaining, base) if the bounds grew.

problemStatement:
Find the number of ways that a given integer **X** can be expressed as the sum of the **N-th powers of unique, natural numbers**.

For example, if `X = 13` and `N = 2`, we have to find the number of ways to express 13 as a sum of squares of unique naturals: `13 = 2² + 3²` is the only way, so the answer is **1**.

Return the count of such representations.
constraints: Naturals used must be unique (each appears at most once)
Order does not matter — {1²,2²} and {2²,1²} are the same representation
The answer is a non-negative integer (0 if no representation exists)
understanding: We are counting subsets of the perfect powers {1^N, 2^N, 3^N, …} whose elements sum to exactly X. 'Unique naturals' means each base is used at most once; 'order does not matter' means we count combinations, not arrangements. Since the bases are tried in strictly increasing order and each base advances the recursion, both conditions are automatically satisfied. The only candidates worth trying are bases up to ⌊X^(1/N)⌋, because beyond that `base^N` already exceeds X.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a number be used more than once, e.g. 2² + 2²?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the naturals must be unique. Advancing the base in both branches enforces this; a base is offered exactly once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does {1², 2²} count differently from {2², 1²}?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Order doesn't matter, so we count combinations. Trying bases in increasing order guarantees each combination is counted once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we return the combinations or just how many there are?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the count. The recursion returns an integer; no need to store the actual subsets.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the base get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only up to ⌊X^(1/N)⌋. Once `base^N > X` no larger base can help, so we prune there — keeping the search tiny.

examples.explanation: 10 = 1² + 3² is the only way (1 + 9 = 10). 10 itself is not a perfect square.
100 = 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + 4³? That's 1+8+27+64 = 100. Exactly one way using cubes.

diagrams.title: Picking the recursion shape
diagrams.caption: Counting unique-power representations is subset-sum's count variant — include/exclude over an increasing base.

approaches.name: Brute Subset Enumeration over Bases
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to frame the problem as 'choose a subset of candidate powers' before collapsing it into the clean recursion.
hints: List the candidate powers: 1^N, 2^N, …, up to the largest base whose power is ≤ X. Call the count m.
Every representation is a subset of those m powers, so enumerate all 2^m subsets (e.g. via bitmasks).
For each subset, sum its powers and increment the count when the sum equals X. Since each power appears once per subset, uniqueness is automatic.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are m ≈ ⌊X^(1/N)⌋ candidate powers, 2^m subsets, and summing a subset costs O(m), giving O(2^m · m). The candidate list is O(m) space.
approaches.explanation:
Make the 'subset of powers' framing literal. First build the candidate list `[1^N, 2^N, …, k^N]` where `k^N ≤ X < (k+1)^N`. Each valid representation is some subset of this list whose elements add up to X, so iterate over all `2^m` subsets and count the ones that hit X exactly.

**Why uniqueness is free.** A subset contains each candidate at most once by definition, so we never reuse a base. And because a subset is unordered, we never double-count `{1², 3²}` and `{3², 1²}`. The two problem constraints fall out of the subset model.

**Why it's only a stepping stone.** Enumerating all `2^m` subsets wastes work: once a partial sum exceeds X, every superset that keeps those elements also exceeds X, yet the bitmask enumeration still visits them. The recursive include/exclude version prunes those branches the instant `base^N > remaining`, which is why it's preferred — but the subset view is the cleanest way to *see* what we're counting.
approaches.insight: Whenever a problem says 'unique elements, order irrelevant, hit a target', it's subset-sum. Enumerating subsets is the brute baseline; pruned recursion is the same enumeration that stops early.

java.line: for (int b = 1; Math.pow(b, N) <= X; b++) powers.add((int) Math.pow(b, N));
java.explanation: Build candidate powers up to the largest base whose power is ≤ X.
Enumerate every subset of the m candidates via bitmask.
Bit i set means candidate i is in this subset.
A subset summing to X is one valid representation.

python.explanation: Collect candidate powers while they don't exceed X.

python.line: total = sum(powers[i] for i in range(m) if mask & (1 << i))
python.explanation: Sum the powers selected by this bitmask.
Count subsets whose power-sum equals X.

pitfalls: Including powers larger than X in the candidate list — wasteful, though they never contribute.
Integer overflow if X were large and N small — fine here (X ≤ 1000).
Visiting all 2^m subsets even after a partial sum exceeds X — no early pruning.

approaches.name: Include/Exclude Recursion with Increasing Base (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Phrase it as 'at each base, take it or skip it, then always advance the base'.
hints: Recurse on `(remaining, base)`. Compute `p = base^N`. If `p == remaining` you've landed exactly on a representation → return 1. If `p > remaining`, no larger base helps → return 0 (prune).
Otherwise make the two choices: **include** `base^N` (recurse with `remaining - p, base + 1`) plus **exclude** it (recurse with `remaining, base + 1`). Sum them.
Always pass `base + 1` so each natural is offered exactly once — that's uniqueness. Start at `ways(X, 1)`.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The recursion branches in two at each base and the base ranges over m ≈ ⌊X^(1/N)⌋ values, so the tree has O(2^m) nodes; the `p > remaining` prune trims many. Each node does O(1) work (a power and a comparison). Recursion depth is O(m).
approaches.explanation:
Frame the search as a sequence of independent yes/no decisions, one per candidate base, taken in increasing order.

**The recursion.** State is `(remaining, base)`: how much of X is left, and the smallest base we're still allowed to use. Compute `p = base^N`.

- If `p == remaining`, using this base exactly finishes a representation → **1 way**.
- If `p > remaining`, this base already overshoots, and every later base is larger, so nothing from here on can work → **0 ways** (this prune is what keeps it fast).
- Otherwise we have a genuine choice: **include** `base^N` (subtract it, advance to `base + 1`) or **exclude** it (keep `remaining`, advance to `base + 1`). The total is the sum of both subtrees.

**Why advancing the base enforces uniqueness.** Both branches recurse with `base + 1`, never `base`. So a base, once considered, is never offered again — each natural is used at most once. And because we only ever move forward, the combination `{1, 3}` is discovered as 'include 1, skip 2, include 3', never as 'include 3, then 1'. That single rule gives us both 'unique' and 'order doesn't matter' for free.

**Why we count instead of collect.** The problem asks only how many representations exist, so each leaf contributes 0 or 1 and we just add. No path array, no copying — the function returns an `int`. If the prompt asked for the actual subsets, we'd carry a list and snapshot it at the `p == remaining` leaf.

**Why no memoization is needed here.** With X ≤ 1000 and N ≥ 2, m = ⌊X^(1/N)⌋ is small (e.g. ≤ 31 for N = 2, X = 1000, and far fewer for larger N), and the overshoot prune cuts the tree hard, so plain recursion is comfortably fast. If the bounds grew, memoizing on `(remaining, base)` would make it pseudo-polynomial.
approaches.insight: This is subset-sum's *count* form: take-it-or-leave-it over candidates, advancing the index so each is used once. The only domain-specific part is generating candidates as perfect powers and pruning when `base^N` overshoots. Recognise the shape and Subsets, Combination Sum, and Partition Equal Subset Sum are the same engine.

dryRun.intro: ways(remaining, base). p = base². Hit when p == remaining, prune when p > remaining. Base advances in both branches.

java.explanation: The current candidate power; recomputed per call (cheap, base is small).

java.line: if (p > remaining) return 0;          // overshoot → no larger base helps
java.explanation: Prune: since bases only grow, once we overshoot nothing further can sum to remaining.

java.line: if (p == remaining) return 1;         // exact hit → one representation
java.explanation: Landing exactly on remaining completes one valid combination.

java.line: return ways(remaining - p, base + 1, N) + ways(remaining, base + 1, N);
java.explanation: Include this power (subtract, advance) plus exclude it (advance) — base+1 enforces uniqueness.

python.explanation: Candidate power for the current base.

python.line:
if p > remaining:
            return 0                      # overshoot → prune
python.explanation: Stop the branch — larger bases only overshoot more.

python.line:
if p == remaining:
            return 1                      # exact hit → one representation
python.explanation: Exact match is a counted representation.

python.line: return ways(remaining - p, base + 1) + ways(remaining, base + 1)
python.explanation: Sum of the include and exclude branches; both move to base + 1.

diagrams.title: Recursion tree for X=10, N=2
diagrams.caption: Left edge = include base², right edge = exclude. The single ✓ leaf is 1² + 3².

edgeCases.behavior: ways(1,1): p = 1 == remaining → return 1. The single base 1 itself is a representation.
ways(2,1): p=1<2 → ways(1,2)+ways(2,2). ways(1,2): p=4>1→0. ways(2,2): p=4>2→0. Total 0 — 2 isn't a sum of unique squares.
Returns 3: 10², 6²+8², and 1²+3²+4²+5²+7² are all found by the increasing-base search.

pitfalls: Recursing with `base` instead of `base + 1` in the include branch — allows reusing a base (e.g. 2²+2²).
Restarting base from 1 each call — produces ordered duplicates and overcounts.
Continuing the search after `base^N > remaining` instead of returning 0 — wasted work and possible miscount.

commonMistakes: Reusing a base by not advancing to base + 1 in the include branch, allowing 2² + 2².
Restarting the base from 1 in each call, which counts the same combination in multiple orders.
Wrong base case — continuing past base^N > remaining instead of pruning, or off-by-one on the exact hit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Allowing a base to be reused
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the include branch recurses with the same base instead of base + 1, the algorithm counts representations like 1² + 1² + … that reuse a natural, violating uniqueness.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return ways(remaining - p, base) + ways(remaining, base + 1)   # base reused!
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return ways(remaining - p, base + 1) + ways(remaining, base + 1)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Restarting the base each call
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping base from 1 inside every call discovers {1,3} as both '1 then 3' and '3 then 1', overcounting. Moving forward only counts each combination once.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the overshoot prune
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without `if (p > remaining) return 0`, the recursion keeps trying ever-larger bases that can never fit, doing pointless work and risking miscounts if the base case is mis-ordered.

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum
followupVariations.hint: Same include/exclude shape, but candidates may be reused — don't advance the index on include.

followupVariations.title: Subsets
followupVariations.hint: Enumerate all subsets with a start index — the structure underlying this count.

followupVariations.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
followupVariations.hint: Subset-sum to a fixed target — same recursion, often memoized into a DP.

patternNote: Include/exclude subset-sum recursion: at each candidate, take it or leave it, advancing the index so each is used at most once. The overshoot prune and exact-hit base case keep it tight. Recognise it whenever you count subsets that hit a target — Combination Sum, Subsets, and Partition Equal Subset Sum share the engine.
